Daniel! I haven't seen you since the audit. How have you been?
Better, thanks. I've been taking my lunch walks, believe it or not.
Good for you. Speaking of which, did you ever book that trip?
We did! We're flying to Chile in March. That reminds me, how was your sister's birthday?
Lovely. She came across as so relaxed, for once. Anyway, how's the new director?
Still a bit hard to read. But going back to Chile, would you recommend Santiago or the south?
The south, without a doubt. On a different note, are you coming to the team dinner on Friday?
I'm not sure yet. To be honest, I'd rather we did it on Saturday.
Speaking of which, did you ever book that trip?
That reminds me, how was your weekend?
Going back to what you said, I agree with you.
On a different note, are you free on Friday?
To sum up, I've been making real progress.

In a real conversation, topics do not wait for permission. They jump. Someone mentions a trip, and a minute later you are talking about their mother, and then about work. Native speakers move between topics with small phrases that act like bridges. Speaking of which connects the new topic to the last one. That reminds me says that something you just heard brought back a memory. By the way adds something small. And when you want to return to an earlier point, going back to what you said is perfect. Without these bridges, a change of topic sounds like a bump. With them, it sounds like a conversation. You do not need many. Three or four, used naturally, are enough to make you sound relaxed, even when you are not.

Somewhere around the middle of learning a language, almost everyone hits a plateau. At the beginning, progress is obvious. Every week you can say things you could not say before. Then, around the intermediate level, the progress becomes invisible. You are still improving, but you cannot feel it, and that is when many people give up. The trick is to measure differently. Do not ask whether you are fluent. Ask smaller questions. Did I speak for two minutes without stopping? Did I change topics without freezing? Did I disagree without apologizing? Record yourself once a month and listen to the old recordings. The difference you cannot feel from week to week is very easy to hear from month to month.

First, I listen to what the other person is talking about, for example a trip. Then I connect a new topic to it: speaking of which, how was your weekend? After that, something they say makes me remember a story: that reminds me of my first job. Next, I return to an earlier point: going back to what you said about work. In the end, I move to something completely new: on a different note, are you free on Friday?
